A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same WorldTest framework and AutumnBench study. Their complete text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support comparison despite extensive reformatting and appendix reorganization.

before.justification: v3 reports original experiments with 517 human participants, reasoning models, simulator and random baselines, plus behavioral and prompt-robustness analyses.

after.justification: v4 retains original empirical results and adds Claude Opus 4.6 evaluation and original exploration, context-use, and cross-benchmark correlation analyses.

M1.justification: WorldTest's two phases and six protocol steps, AutumnBench's three challenge procedures, and the simulator solvers remain unchanged. The explicit query definition and expanded explanations do not introduce a new algorithm or model component.

E1.justification: The same 43 environments, 129 tasks, and human population are retained; Appendix B's expanded taxonomy redescribes existing environments. v4 adds secondary evaluation data comprising published software-engineering, terminal-use, science, and mathematics benchmark scores for construct-validity analysis in F.4. These are score comparisons, not newly executed external benchmark tasks.

E2.justification: v4 adds Claude Opus 4.6 across the AutumnBench problems in Table F.2. Gemini 2.5 Flash and Qwen already appear in v3's Table E.2 and figures, despite its abstract mentioning three models. The other reasoning, human, simulator, and random comparators are retained.

E3.justification: New analyses introduce rule-coverage measurement, reset-comparison windows spanning 6% of interaction length clipped to 10–50 actions, difficulty-controlled context analysis, and external rank correlations. The reported stochasticity grouping also changes, including classifying 7VKTD as deterministic. Existing task scoring and human aggregation remain unchanged; Opus uses the existing single-trajectory protocol.

E4.justification: v4 substantially expands diagnostics through causal-rule coverage, pre/post-reset sequence similarity, context-length and usage analyses, and cross-benchmark construct-validity correlations. It removes v3 E.4.2's pooled and per-agent perplexity–performance analyses. Existing prompt robustness, computational-cost analysis, random-agent difficulty results, and the qualitative trace remain.

E5.justification: Table F.4 newly reports reset-similarity medians, middle-95% ranges, and Mann–Whitney U tests for human–model differences. Existing repeated-run counts and prompt-table uncertainty reporting are retained; the PDFs do not establish an increase in repetitions.

E6.justification: v4 adds Opus results, including 39.9% overall, and coverage, reset, context, and external-correlation findings. Reset LCS means are newly reported as 0.637 for humans versus 0.188–0.360 for models. Figure 5 changes human reset/no-op shares from approximately 12.5% to 7.2% each, and Figure 6 revises human distributions. Existing per-environment scores, prompt results, and random probabilities remain unchanged; the old perplexity-correlation results disappear.

T1.justification: Section 4.1 newly defines an environment-level query as a computable higher-order function q mapping environments to answers. The existing POMDP framework, challenge-scoring mathematics, perplexity definitions, and next-state-model derivations are retained, with no new proof.

C1.justification: The abstract adds the explicit claim that individual queries can target properties undetermined by any single rollout distribution and emphasizes generality across query types. The principal contributions—WorldTest, AutumnBench, and the human–model performance gap—remain the same.

C2.justification: v4 adds interpretations connecting rule coverage and reset structure to experimentation, and external correlations to transferable capabilities. It explicitly qualifies causal attribution, discusses prompt sensitivity and small correlation samples, and distinguishes the simulator's claimed prediction bound from its limited planning baseline. Conversely, it removes v3's qualification that perplexity weakly predicts success despite retaining perplexity-based learning interpretations.

D1.justification: v4 supplies explicit interpreter and baseline repository locations and a named public dataset release. It newly documents five same-type problems per human participant, model context-window capacities, and thinking-token handling. These disclosures supplement retained prompts, interfaces, and baseline implementation details.

R1.justification: Related work expands two-phase evaluation to include in-context RL through Laskin et al. (2023). Additional cognitive-science, context-learning, and external-benchmark references support the new analyses. The main positioning against static, representation-based, reward-driven, and two-phase benchmarks remains intact.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, framework exposition, and substantial discussion passages are rewritten around environment-level queries. Appendix B receives an expanded taxonomy, while the former Appendix E is reorganized into reference theory/baselines and a separate results Appendix F. Availability information also receives a dedicated section.

P2.justification: v4 adopts a two-column main-text layout, redraws the overview, rearranges Figure 6 and corrects its caption, and restructures environment and random-baseline tables. It adds category, reset, context, and external-comparison tables, expands the score table with Opus columns, and removes the perplexity-correlation tables.

improvement.justification: v4 improves formal clarity, baseline currency, exploration diagnostics, access information, and causal qualification. However, it removes v3's weak/null perplexity-validation evidence while retaining the associated learning claims, and introduces inconsistent summaries: F.1.1 reports 12 universally unsolved environments whereas Table F.2 shows six; Figure 5's revised human proportions also conflict with the retained 12.5% prose. These substantive benefits and reporting harms prevent a reliable net-quality judgment.
